titel: Cash flow and the cash flow statement
kurz: Why profit, as an allocation to periods, can differ from the payments in the bank account, and how to analyse this difference.

bloecke.md:
A company can report a profit three years in a row and still file for insolvency. The reason lies in the logic of bookkeeping. Revenue counts as realised when delivery has taken place and the consideration is as good as certain, and not only when the money comes in (realisation principle, Section 252 of the Commercial Code, HGB). Depreciation and provisions reduce profit without any payment being made. The largest cash outflow of many companies, investment in machinery, software or buildings, appears in the income statement only as depreciation spread over several years.

Profit plays no role in the grounds for insolvency. Inability to pay (Zahlungsunfähigkeit) under Section 17 of the Insolvency Code (InsO) and over-indebtedness (Überschuldung) under Section 19 InsO concern liquidity and assets, not the result. The cash flow statement is therefore the cross-check within the financial statements. It translates the result back into payments and shows how much of it is left.

## The three sections of the cash flow statement

Every payment is allocated to one of three sections (IAS 7, specified in more detail for German consolidated financial statements by German Accounting Standard DRS 21). In consolidated financial statements, the cash flow statement is always a mandatory component (Section 297(1) HGB); in single-entity financial statements, it is mandatory only for capital-market-oriented corporations that are not required to prepare consolidated financial statements (Section 264(1) sentence 2 HGB).

- **Operating cash flow** comprises all payments from ongoing business, that is, receipts from customers, materials, wages, taxes and usually also interest.
- **Investing cash flow** comprises the purchase and sale of property, plant and equipment, intangible assets, equity investments and financial investments. For a company that continues its operations, it is permanently negative. If it is permanently positive, the company is selling off its asset base.
- **Financing cash flow** comprises taking out and repaying loans, capital increases, dividends and share buybacks.

The sum of the three sections gives the change in cash and cash equivalents. This figure alone says little; what is revealing is its composition. When comparing the sections, you should check how payments have been classified. IAS 7 allows latitude for interest and dividends paid and received, and companies use it differently. From the 2027 financial year, IFRS 18 standardises the presentation and restricts such options.

## The indirect method

Two presentations are permitted, and in practice the indirect one predominates. It starts with the profit for the period and works backwards. Everything that reduced or increased profit without touching the bank account is stripped out. In addition, everything that tied up or released cash without appearing in profit is taken into account.

bloecke.formel: Operating cash flow = net profit + non-cash expenses − non-cash income − increase in working capital
bloecke.erklaerung: Non-cash expenses are mainly depreciation, additions to provisions and share-based payment. The direct method, that is, cash receipts minus cash payments, would be more informative. However, it requires the cash flows to be recorded separately and is therefore rare.

## Working capital as the cause of the difference

Growth costs money at first, and the receipts only follow later. A company that wants to sell more has to hold more goods in stock, and as sales grow, so do customers' unpaid invoices. Both tie up capital. Only the company's own trade payables work against this, because invoices not yet paid are like an interest-free loan. Three ratios measure this in days: days sales outstanding (DSO), days inventory outstanding (DIO) and days payables outstanding (DPO).

bloecke.formel: Cash conversion cycle = DIO + DSO − DPO
bloecke.erklaerung: The cash conversion cycle states in days how long capital is tied up between paying the supplier and receiving the money from the customer. A negative value means that the customer pays before the supplier is paid. In food retail and subscription models, this is the norm and a financing advantage; in plant engineering, by contrast, it is unattainable.
variablen: average trade payables / cost of sales × 365

bloecke.titel: Capital tied up per day of payment terms
bloecke.md:
With annual revenue of €720 million, one day of DSO corresponds to about 720 / 365 = €1.97 million of capital tied up. If DSO rises from 52.5 to 60 days, this deterioration alone ties up about €15 million, on top of the capital tied up by revenue growth. In total, receivables in the model grow by €32.1 million, and operating cash flow is lower by this amount.

The reverse also applies. A company that wants to improve its cash flow for a quarter can shorten its customers' payment terms, pay suppliers later or sell receivables. That is not fraud, but it does not improve the business either. It is a one-off release of capital that cannot be repeated.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation in € million with 20% revenue growth a year, a constant 8% net margin, depreciation of 6% and capital expenditure of 9% of revenue; DSO rises from 45 to 75 days.

bloecke.md:
This company is not automatically in trouble. It is pre-financing its growth, and if the investments later generate revenue with a higher return on capital, that was the right decision. It only becomes a problem if growth fails to materialise but the capital remains tied up, or if the gap is permanently closed with new debt. What needs to be clarified, therefore, is which items explain the difference between profit and cash flow and whether they are one-off or structural.

The most robust check is a ratio over several years: operating cash flow divided by net profit. If it is clearly below one on average over five or ten years, without growth or a build-up of working capital explaining this, something is wrong with the quality of earnings. Piotroski uses this idea in one of his nine criteria, according to which operating cash flow should exceed net profit.

## Maintenance and growth capex

Investing cash flow does not show what the money was invested in. A company that only replaces its assets and one that builds a second plant look the same in this line. A first approximation is the comparison with depreciation, which measures the scheduled consumption of the existing asset base. If capital expenditure stays below depreciation over the long term, the asset base is shrinking, and cash flow only looks good because nothing is being replaced. If it is well above depreciation, the company is growing or catching up on postponed investment.

The second check concerns capitalisation. A company that capitalises development costs shifts a cash outflow from operating cash flow to investing cash flow. Operating cash flow and profit rise as a result, while free cash flow remains unchanged. Under IAS 38, capitalisation is even mandatory once the criteria are met; under Section 248(2) HGB it is an option. That is why capital expenditure and own work capitalised are always considered together with operating cash flow.

If development costs, software or other own work are capitalised instead of being expensed, the cash outflow merely shifts into investing cash flow.

Under IFRS 16, lessees have had to recognise leases on the balance sheet for financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2019. Rental expense becomes depreciation and interest, and the repayment portion of the lease payment appears in financing cash flow. EBITDA and operating cash flow rise as a result, without a single extra euro being earned. Time series spanning 2019 are not meaningful without adjustment.

Measures taken shortly before the balance sheet date also lift operating cash flow, such as factoring or reverse factoring, delayed payments to suppliers or early payments from customers. This only becomes visible when you place DSO and DPO for several years side by side.

In addition, there is share-based payment. It is non-cash and is therefore added back in operating cash flow. The cost is nevertheless borne by the existing shareholders, because the number of shares increases.

## Owner earnings and the four free cash flow concepts

Free cash flow is not defined in any accounting standard. The usual calculation is operating cash flow minus capital expenditure on property, plant and equipment and intangible assets. When comparing companies, you have to look up the definition in the annual report. Some companies deduct only replacement investment, some strip out lease repayments, others add in proceeds from disposals.

In Berkshire's 1986 annual report, Buffett proposed a figure that starts at this point. It consists of reported earnings plus depreciation and other non-cash charges, less the average annual capital expenditure needed to maintain unit volume and competitive position. Only maintenance capex is deducted, not growth capex. Buffett noted in the same passage that this last item must be a guess, and sometimes one that is very difficult to make. The figure is therefore imprecise, but it does not pretend to a precision that does not exist.

bloecke.md: Over the entire life of a company, the sum of its profits equals the sum of its cash surpluses. Differences in individual periods are timing shifts that are either economically justified or brought about by accounting policy. The analysis consists of separating these two cases.

bloecke.titel: Checks for the cash flow statement
bloecke.md:
1. Operating cash flow divided by net profit, over five to ten years, as individual years say little.
2. Capital expenditure compared with depreciation, also over several years. This separates maintenance from growth and from erosion of the asset base.
3. Free cash flow compared with dividends and share buybacks. If more is paid out than generated over the long term, the rest comes from debt or from the asset base.
4. The working capital line compared with revenue growth. If capital tied up grows faster than revenue, that needs explaining.

bloecke.titel: Limits of the cash flow statement
bloecke.md: For banks and insurers, the cash flow statement says very little. Cash itself is the subject of their business, and operating cash flow fluctuates with deposit and lending business without saying anything about earning power. For real estate companies, too, the figures are hard to interpret, because valuation gains dominate the result but never turn into cash. There, the sector works with its own measures such as FFO (funds from operations). For young companies without profits, operating cash flow mainly shows how long the existing money will last.

mitnehmen: Solvency and quality of earnings can be assessed from the cash flow statement, because it shows payments, whereas the income statement allocates income and expenses to periods.
The difference between profit and operating cash flow almost always arises from depreciation, provisions and working capital and can be explained item by item.
Free cash flow is not defined, so before any comparison you check how the company calculates it.
Capitalisation, IFRS 16 and reporting-date effects increase operating cash flow without improving the business.
Owner earnings deducts only maintenance capex and is therefore closer to the amount an owner could withdraw permanently, but it relies on an estimate.

begriffe.text: The cash surplus from ongoing business. Under the indirect method, it is derived from net profit, plus non-cash expenses and less the increase in working capital.

Operating cash flow less capital expenditure on property, plant and equipment and intangible assets. The figure is not defined by law, so you have to look up how the company in question calculates it.
A figure proposed by Buffett in 1986, made up of profit plus non-cash charges, less the average capital expenditure needed to maintain unit volume and competitive position.
The part of capital expenditure that merely keeps existing operations going. It is not reported separately; scheduled depreciation serves as a first approximation.

Days inventory outstanding plus days sales outstanding minus days payables outstanding, in days. The ratio measures how long capital is tied up between paying the supplier and receiving the money from the customer.
